729.title: Cyril of Jerusalem's lectures
729.hook: talks to the newly baptized explaining what they had just experienced
729.howItsDone: In the Catholic Church the time after adult baptism at the Easter Vigil is called mystagogy: the newly baptized keep meeting during the Easter season to reflect on the sacraments they have received.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephrem, the deacon who set the faith to music and taught choirs to sing it. Your line was theology you can sing.

Jerusalem, the days after Easter. A group of people come back to church who were baptized only days ago. They had been taught the creed and the stories, but nobody had walked them through what would actually happen to them. They went in, and it happened: words, oil, water, bread. Now they sit down, still a little dazed, and the bishop stands up. In effect he says: you've been through it. Now I'll tell you what it meant. The talks known as Cyril's lectures to the newly baptized are that explanation.
screen: `BAPTIZED A FEW DAYS AGO.` → `NOBODY EXPLAINED IT BEFOREHAND.` → `NOW, WHAT IT MEANT.`

segments.voice: These talks have a name: mystagogy. The first thing the bishop says explains the order. He had long wanted to speak to them about these mysteries, but seeing persuades more than hearing, so he waited until they had seen for themselves. First the night. Then the words. Then he walks them back through it. Remember, he says, how you stood in the outer hall, facing west, the direction of darkness, stretched out your hand and renounced Satan. Then you turned to the east, toward the light. Remember how you took off your old garment, were anointed with oil, were led to the pool, and were asked whether you believed in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Every gesture had a meaning, and now he gives it to them. Then the altar. He quotes the psalm sung at communion. In the Douay-Rheims it reads: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet." And he gives a very practical instruction. When you come forward, don't come with your fingers spread. Make your left hand a throne for the right, because the right hand is about to receive a King. Hollow your palm, receive the Body of Christ, and answer Amen. The Catechism of the Catholic Church uses the word mystagogy for teaching that moves from the visible to the invisible, from the sign to the thing it signifies. The water, the oil, the open hand.
screen: `FIRST THE NIGHT, THEN THE WORDS.` · `TURN FROM THE WEST TO THE EAST.` · `A THRONE FOR THE KING.` · `FROM THE SIGN TO WHAT IT SIGNIFIES.` · then, large: `O TASTE, AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Pick a sacrament you've received or watched, a baptism, communion, a wedding, an anointing, or, if you're new to all this, a ritual you've seen at a wedding or a funeral. Walk through it one piece at a time, water, oil, a ring, bread in an open hand, and ask of each: what is this pointing to? If you're not sure, just let the question stay.
Mystagogy. Teaching given after the rite, leading the newly baptized from what they saw to what it means. Today's word.
Your line: after, the meaning. First the night, then the words that explain it. Until tomorrow.

730.title: Martin's cloak (c. 316–397)
730.hook: a soldier cuts his cloak in half for a beggar and dreams of Christ wearing it
730.howItsDone: Catholics honor Martin of Tours as a saint; in parts of Europe his feast is kept with lantern processions and shared food, and some parishes run coat and blanket drives as winter begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril's lectures and the word mystagogy: first the night, then the words. Your line was after, the meaning.

A winter so cold, Sulpicius says, that people were dying of it. A young soldier named Martin rides up to the gate of the city of Amiens. At the gate stands a man with no clothes at all, asking the people going in and out for help. They pass him. Martin has already given away what else he had. All that's left is the cloak on his back and the sword at his side. And he looks at the cloak, and then at the sword.
screen: `A WINTER GATE.` → `A MAN WITH NOTHING.` → `A CLOAK AND A SWORD.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Sulpicius Severus, who wrote a life of Martin and says he knew him. Martin draws his sword, cuts the cloak in two, gives one half to the man, and wraps himself in what's left. Notice the half. He doesn't hand over the whole thing and ride off a hero. He shares it, and goes on looking a little ridiculous. Sulpicius says some of the bystanders laughed at how he looked. Others were ashamed, because they had more to give and hadn't given it. Then the night. Martin is asleep, and in a dream he sees Christ, wearing the half of the cloak he gave away. He's told to look closely and recognize it. And he hears Christ say to the angels around him, more or less: Martin, who is still only a catechumen, clothed me with this. A catechumen is someone still preparing for baptism. Martin wasn't even baptized yet. Sulpicius ties the dream to words of Jesus in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Martin, Sulpicius says, didn't grow proud over the dream. He took it as a push, and went to be baptized. So the story has two halves, like the cloak: a man at a gate, and Christ in the dream, wearing the same piece of cloth. The Catholic Church remembers Martin as a saint, a soldier who later became a monk and a bishop.

If you pray, remember that person by name, or by the place they stand.

Your line: half a cloak. You don't have to give everything; half counts. Day seven hundred thirty, done.

731.title: Ambrose (c. 339–397)
731.hook: the crowd shouts Ambrose for bishop before he's even baptized
731.howItsDone: Catholics honor Ambrose as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and Milan's own liturgical tradition, the Ambrosian rite, still bears his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin's cloak: one half for the man at the gate, one half for Martin. Your line was half a cloak.

The church in Milan is about to turn into a riot. The bishop has died, and the city has to choose a new one. Two parties are packed inside, shouting: those who follow the teaching of Arius, and those who hold to the creed of Nicaea, the same quarrel we met in the Arian question. So the governor of the province comes down himself to keep the peace, a trained lawyer and a public official. His name is Ambrose. He stands up and starts talking the room down. And then, over his voice, somebody shouts his name.
screen: `A CHURCH ABOUT TO RIOT.` → `THE GOVERNOR COMES TO KEEP THE PEACE.` → `SOMEBODY SHOUTS HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: The account comes from Paulinus, who served as Ambrose's secretary and wrote his life after his death. Paulinus says that while Ambrose was speaking, a child's voice cried out: Ambrose, bishop! And the whole crowd took it up. Both parties, who agreed on nothing, suddenly agreed on him. Here's the catch. Ambrose was not a priest. He wasn't even baptized. He was a catechumen, still preparing for baptism, a public official with a career. So he tried to get out of it, and some of the attempts are almost comic. He tried acting harsh in court, to seem unfit. He slipped out of the city by night, heading for another town, and, Paulinus says, wandered all night and found himself at the gate of Milan in the morning. He hid at a friend's country estate, and the friend gave him up. In the end he said yes. He was baptized, and days later made bishop. Later Ambrose wrote about it himself, in a book on the duties of the clergy. He says he was carried off from the judge's bench and the robes of office into the priesthood, and so he began to teach before he had learned. He had to learn and teach at the same time. A bishop, putting that in writing. He wasn't ready, he said so, and he took the job anyway, learning as he went.
screen: `A CHILD'S VOICE: AMBROSE, BISHOP!` · `HE TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.` · `BAPTIZED, THEN MADE BISHOP.` · `TEACHING BEFORE LEARNING.` · then, large: `CHOSEN BEFORE READY.`

segments.voice: Name one thing in front of you that you keep stepping around because you don't feel qualified: a role at work, looking after a parent, leading something small. Notice the reasons you've been giving for saying no, then picture the first small step you could take while you learn. If you pray, ask for help with it.
Ambrose. The governor in Milan whom a crowd made bishop before he was baptized, and who said he had to learn and teach at the same time. Today's word.
Your line: chosen before ready. Being ready can come along the way, as you learn. See you tomorrow.

732.title: Ambrose and the emperor
732.hook: after a massacre, Ambrose makes the emperor do public penance
732.howItsDone: Catholics confess serious sin in the sacrament of penance, also called reconciliation; public penance like the emperor's belongs to the early Church, and today the sacrament is ordinarily private, between penitent and priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose, made bishop by a shouting crowd before he was even baptized. Your line was chosen before ready.

A letter, written by hand, meant for one reader. The reader is the emperor Theodosius, a Christian, and a man who comes to church in Milan. The writer is the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. Something terrible has happened in the city of Thessalonica. After a riot there, the emperor's soldiers turned on the people of the city and killed them. The emperor is expected at Mass as usual. And the bishop has to decide what to say to him.
screen: `A LETTER FOR ONE READER.` → `A MASSACRE IN THESSALONICA.` → `THE EMPEROR EXPECTS MASS AS USUAL.`

segments.voice: Ambrose's letter is quieter than the legend. He doesn't denounce the emperor from the pulpit. He writes privately, and he writes as a pastor. He grieves over Thessalonica. He tells Theodosius plainly that he dare not offer the sacrifice of the Mass if the emperor intends to be there, not with this on his hands. And he points him to someone the emperor would know from scripture: King David. After David sent a man to his death, the prophet Nathan confronted him, and David didn't argue. In the Douay-Rheims: "And David said to Nathan: I have sinned against the Lord." Ambrose's message, more or less: a king did this before you. You can do it too. And Theodosius did. Ambrose describes it later, in the sermon he preached at the emperor's funeral. The emperor laid aside the signs of his royal rank, wept for his sin openly in church, and asked for pardon. Public penance, done by an emperor. Here's where the story grows. A later historian, Theodoret, tells a more dramatic version: Ambrose meets the emperor at the church door and blocks his way in front of everyone. Ambrose's own letter is private and patient. Both versions agree on the ending, though. The emperor stood among sinners and asked for mercy.

733.title: Monica's tears (Confessions 3)
733.hook: a mother prays for years for her son; a bishop tells her a son of such tears can't be lost
733.howItsDone: Catholics honor Monica as a saint and some ask her prayers for children who have drifted from the faith; her feast falls the day before her son Augustine's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose and the emperor, and paenitentia: a private letter, King David's words, and an emperor who laid aside his rank. Your line was even the emperor.

Augustine wrote his Confessions talking to God, not to us. We're overhearing. And in the third book he remembers his mother, crying. He's a young man, brilliant, restless, and he has joined a religious movement called the Manichees, whose teaching he later left behind. His mother, Monica, is a Christian, and she weeps over him, he says, more than mothers weep over a child's dead body. He's writing this long afterward, and he sets her tears down in a book addressed to God.
screen: `A BOOK WRITTEN TO GOD.` → `A SON GONE ANOTHER WAY.` → `A MOTHER WHO WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Augustine tells two moments. First, a dream. Monica dreams she's standing on a wooden ruler, grieving, and a young man, bright and smiling, comes up and asks why she's sad. She says she's mourning her son's ruin. He tells her to look: where she is, there her son is too. She looks, and sees Augustine standing beside her on the same ruler. When she tells him, Augustine tries to twist it: maybe it means she'll come round to where he is. She answers straight away: no. It didn't say where he is, you are. It said where you are, he is. Augustine admits her quick answer moved him more than the dream did. Second, a bishop, whom Augustine doesn't name. Monica begs him to talk with her son and argue him out of his errors. The bishop refuses. The young man is too pleased with his new ideas, he says. Let him alone. Only pray for him. He'll find out by reading. The bishop even tells her he went down that same road as a boy, and found his own way out. But Monica keeps pressing, and crying. Finally, a little annoyed, the bishop says the line Augustine wrote down. Go your way: it cannot be that the son of these tears should be lost. Augustine says she took it as if it had sounded from heaven. Notice what the bishop didn't do. He didn't argue with the son. He sent the mother back to her prayers.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who feels far from you right now, far in miles, or gone quiet, gone another direction. Don't argue with them in your head; just hold them, and say their name. If you pray, place them before God the way Monica did; if you don't, keep them in mind, warmly, without fixing anything.
Monica's tears. A mother's prayers for her son Augustine, and a bishop's promise that the son of such tears could not be lost. Today's word.

734.title: The pears (Confessions 2)
734.hook: young Augustine steals pears he doesn't want, just for the thrill
734.howItsDone: Catholics prepare for confession with an examination of conscience, looking back over what they have done and why; Augustine's Confessions is read as an example of that kind of honest look.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Monica's tears, and a bishop who told her the son of such tears could not be lost. Your line was the son of these tears.

A pear tree, next to a vineyard, loaded with fruit. And the pears, Augustine tells us, weren't even good: nothing special to look at, nothing special to eat. We step back a book now, to Book Two of the Confessions, when he's still a boy at home. Late one night, after hanging around the streets, he and a gang of friends go to that tree. They shake it. They haul off armloads of pears. They aren't hungry. They don't want pears. Long afterward, as he writes, this small theft is still bothering him.
screen: `A PEAR TREE BY A VINEYARD.` → `THE PEARS WEREN'T EVEN GOOD.` → `A GANG, LATE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's what they did with the pears. They ate a few, Augustine says, and threw the rest to the pigs. He had better pears at home. So why? That's the whole question of the passage, and he won't let it go. The only pleasure in it, he says, was that it wasn't allowed. He loved not the pears, but the wrong itself. Then he goes looking for a motive the way a detective would. People who do terrible things, he says, usually want something: another man's wife, his land, money to live on, revenge. Even a cruel man has a reason. He can't find his. Then he finds one piece. He would not have done it alone. Alone, he says, it would have been no fun at all. It was the laughing together, the dare, the being in on it. He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. Some readers hear an echo of another garden here, the tree in Genesis, fruit taken because it was forbidden. The loads were heavy, he says, but the stakes were nothing. Pears nobody wanted. Pig food. That's why it works. A big crime has big reasons. A pointless wrong shows the heart with nothing else in the way. And notice the tone. No list of punishments, no big drama. He's asking, in front of God, a question that's easy to skip: why did I do it?
screen: `NOT HUNGRY, NOT EVEN GOOD PEARS.` · `HE LOVED THE WRONG ITSELF.` · `ALONE, HE WOULDN'T HAVE DONE IT.` · `A SMALL WRONG SHOWS THE HEART.` · then, large: `WHY DID I DO IT?`

segments.voice: Not your worst moment: let one small wrong come up, with no good reason behind it, a cruel joke, something broken for fun, a rumor passed on because it was juicy. Ask Augustine's question quietly, why did I do it, who was I with, what did I want, and don't punish yourself; just look. If you pray, name it to God, the way Augustine did.
The pears. A small theft from Augustine's boyhood, pears he didn't want, taken with friends for the thrill of the forbidden. Today's word.
Your line: why did I do it. An honest question, asked gently and without punishment. Until tomorrow.

A job offer. The city of Milan needs a teacher of public speaking, and Augustine gets the post. He's a professional now: he teaches young men how to persuade a room. He arrives in Milan and, as part of settling in, goes to meet the bishop. It's Ambrose, the governor the crowd made bishop, the one who wrote to the emperor. Augustine has heard Ambrose is a superb speaker. So when Ambrose preaches, he goes to church. Not to pray. To review the performance.
screen: `A NEW JOB IN MILAN.` → `A PROFESSIONAL PERSUADER.` → `HE GOES TO REVIEW THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: Augustine tells it in Books Five and Six of the Confessions. First, the welcome. Ambrose received him like a father, and Augustine began to love him, not yet as a teacher of truth, he admits, just as a man who was kind to him. Then the sermons. Augustine sits there like a critic. Is the bishop as good as his reputation? He listens closely to the words and doesn't care about the content. He even enjoys the sweetness of the speaking. And then something happens he didn't plan. While he was opening his ears to how well Ambrose spoke, he says, how truly he spoke came in along with it, little by little. He couldn't separate the two. He came for the style, and the substance got in. One thing that got in was a way of reading the Old Testament. Augustine had found some of its stories crude. Ambrose kept repeating a line from Saint Paul. In the Douay-Rheims: "the letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth." Read for the spirit, and the hard passages opened up. And one more picture from Milan: Ambrose reading. His eyes moved over the page, his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were still. Augustine and his friends would come in, find him reading silently, sit a while without disturbing him, and leave. He wanted to talk to the bishop and couldn't get the time. He got the sermons instead.
